tldr: For nonlinear systems facing intermittent sensor measurements—such as in visual servoing or wireless setups—this paper proposes a convex MPC method. It globally linearizes the dynamics via a deep Koopman model, models measurement dropouts and resets as a Markov jump system, and theoretically guarantees recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability.
overview:
In visual servoing with cameras or teleoperated robots, sensor measurements often drop out intermittently due to leaving the camera's field of view (FOV), occlusions, or communication hiccups. If you try to control the robot safely with nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC), prediction errors balloon while observations are gone. Even worse, the moment a measurement returns, the state resets discontinuously. This often leads to a "loss of recursive feasibility" where the optimization problem becomes unsolvable, causing computational failure.

To solve this, the authors developed a novel stochastic MPC framework combining a deep Koopman model—which embeds nonlinear dynamics into a latent linear space—with a two-mode Markov chain that represents measurement availability. They formulated both the error accumulation during dropouts and the abrupt state jumps from resets into a unified Markov jump error dynamic. Under numerically verifiable conditions, they proved that the prediction error remains mean-square ultimately bounded (MSUB).

Furthermore, to avoid over-tightening constraints from overly cautious worst-case assumptions, they introduced a distribution-free probabilistic error radius to truncate constraint tightening. They also incorporated an exact-penalty soft-constraint mechanism to absorb abrupt shifts during state resets. This preserves the online optimization as a fast quadratic program (QP) while reconciling theoretical stability and feasibility. In a visual tracking simulation on a 2-DOF gimbal with flexible joints, the method achieved impressive high-speed computation averaging 2.0 ms along with robust tracking performance.
contributions: Reduced online optimization to a convex quadratic program (QP) by using a Lipschitz-constrained deep Koopman model to embed nonlinear dynamics into a tractable linear latent space.

Modeled measurement dropouts (open-loop propagation) and recoveries (measurement-triggered resets) as a unified Markov jump error system, deriving verifiable sufficient conditions for mean-square ultimate boundedness (MSUB) of prediction errors alongside explicit error bounds.

Theoretically proved recursive feasibility and closed-loop stability by introducing probabilistic truncation to prevent over-tightening during prolonged dropouts, together with exact-penalty soft constraints to absorb abrupt state resets.

sections.heading: Why Intermittent Measurements Break Nonlinear MPC
sections.summary: While MPC shines in handling multivariable constraints in robot control, temporary losses of sensor feedback cause prediction errors to explode, leaving solvers with no feasible solution. This section describes the motivation for combining Koopman operators with a stochastic approach to overcome the computational burden and conservatism of conventional nonlinear and tube MPC.
sections.details:
Model predictive control (MPC) is widely used across robotics because it explicitly handles state and control constraints during optimization. However, standard MPC assumes uninterrupted feedback at every single step. In real-world robot navigation or visual servoing, sensor data drops out probabilistically all the time due to field-of-view (FOV) exits, occlusions, or temporary wireless drops.

While robust nonlinear MPC (NMPC) can preserve safety for nonlinear systems, solving nonconvex optimization problems in real time is computationally prohibitive. Recently, Koopman operator theory has gained traction because it lifts nonlinear dynamics into a higher-dimensional linear space. Once lifted to a linear state space, problems can be solved rapidly as quadratic programs (QPs). Deep learning-based deep Koopman methods have also drastically boosted the expressive power for complex functional spaces.

Still, what happens when measurements drop out for an extended period? If you keep expanding error tubes to account for the worst case, as in traditional tube MPC, constraint tightening becomes excessively strict. You quickly face a "loss of recursive feasibility," where no feasible solution exists. In addition, resetting nominal states with actual measurements right when feedback returns introduces sudden state jumps that confound optimization solvers. This paper introduces a new control framework that tackles this triple challenge of nonlinearity, stochastic measurement dropouts, and strict safety constraints simultaneously.

sections.heading: Lifting to Koopman Latent Space and Modeling with Markov Jumps
sections.summary: Using a Lipschitz-constrained neural network, the nonlinear system is mapped to a latent linear space, and the presence of measurements is modeled as a two-mode Markov chain. This unifies open-loop propagation during dropouts and state resets upon recovery into a single Markov jump system.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Linearization via Koopman Operator and Nominal MPC
The controlled plant is a nonlinear discrete-time system with input: $x_{k+1} = F(x_k, u_k)$. The authors adopt a deep Koopman model whose observable functions are trained via a neural network. For the latent state $z_k = [x_k^T, \psi(x_k)^T]^T$, a skip connection is placed on the first $n_x$ dimensions to retain the original state $x_k$ directly, while the remaining $n_\psi$ dimensions are assigned to the nonlinear features $\psi(x_k)$. This clever setup eliminates the need for nonlinear decoding calculations to reconstruct the state; the original state is extracted simply via a projection matrix $C = [I_{n_x}, \mathbf{0}]$.
Furthermore, spectral normalization is applied to each network layer, globally restricting the mapping's Lipschitz constant to $1$ or less. Additionally, an eigenvalue penalty term and an orthogonal regularization term are added to the loss function to ensure the latent system matrix $A$ remains Schur stable (all eigenvalues have absolute values strictly less than 1).

### 2.2 Deriving Error Bounds in Latent Space
In practice, modeling errors and environmental disturbances $w_k$ are unavoidable. The authors analyzed how bounded uncertainties in the state space propagate into the latent space based on Lipschitz continuity. As a result, they proved that the upper bound on the prediction error norm in the high-dimensional latent space can be evaluated geometrically using low-dimensional error norms and encoder consistency residuals (Lemma 2.1).

### 2.3 Markov Jump Modeling of Intermittent Measurements
Measurement availability is modeled as a discrete-time Markov chain with a mode variable $\theta_k \in \{0, 1\}$. Here, $\theta_k=0$ indicates noisy but available measurements, while $\theta_k=1$ indicates a measurement dropout. On steps where measurements recover, the nominal state is reset using the latent state derived from actual observations; during dropouts, open-loop propagation continues with the nominal model. The authors unified these two behaviors cleanly into a single non-homogeneous Markov jump error dynamic, where system matrices and disturbances switch depending on the next step's observation mode $\theta_{k+1}$.

sections.heading: Theoretical Guarantees: Mean-Square Boundedness and Probabilistic Soft Constraints
sections.summary: Lyapunov analysis on the Markov jump system yields conditions for prediction errors to be mean-square ultimately bounded (MSUB), enabling the construction of a probabilistic safety radius for any confidence level. Pairing this with soft constraints mathematically guarantees that the QP solver will always stay feasible despite dropouts.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Open-Loop Error Growth and Constraint Tightening
When measurements are lost for $l$ consecutive steps, the open-loop prediction error set $\mathcal{E}_l$ expands like a snowball over time. If state constraints are tightened inward accordingly, the admissible region shrinks to an empty set, causing the MPC to crash due to infeasibility.

### 3.2 Mean-Square Ultimate Boundedness (MSUB) of Prediction Errors
Even if errors grow locally, they should not blow up over long horizons if measurements statistically return eventually ($p_{11} < 1$). By constructing a mode-dependent quadratic Lyapunov function, the authors rigorously proved via linear matrix inequality (LMI) feasibility that the latent prediction error is mean-square ultimately bounded (MSUB) (Theorem 3.3). This yields an explicit steady-state upper bound $E_\infty^2$ on the error's second moment.

### 3.3 Recursive Feasibility via Probabilistic Truncation and Soft Constraints
Using the derived error bound along with Markov's inequality, they compute a distribution-free probabilistic error radius $R_{prob}$ satisfying a specified confidence level $p$ (e.g., 95%). They then introduce "probabilistic truncation," which caps the tightening of constraints at $R_{prob}$ no matter how long dropouts persist.
Furthermore, to cushion the shock of abrupt state resets triggered by new measurements, they formulate the optimization problem $\mathcal{P}_N^{soft}$ using $L_1$ exact-penalty soft constraints (slack variables $\epsilon$). Setting the penalty coefficient sufficiently large allows the controller to act like a hard-constrained system in normal operation, while flexibly using slack during measurement resets or extended outages to keep the problem feasible. Under stated terminal invariant compatibility conditions, they proved that this optimization problem remains feasible over future steps (recursive feasibility) and that closed-loop tracking errors also achieve MSUB (Theorem 3.6).

captions.F2: Figure F2 shows the cloverleaf curve (reference trajectory) on the image plane used for verification. The path features sharp turns sweeping outward from near the origin, presenting a challenging setup that tests tracking performance under both strong nonlinearity and field-of-view (FOV) constraints.

sections.heading: Validation on a 2-DOF Elastic-Joint Gimbal: 95% Safety Guarantee and 2 ms Ultra-Fast Computation
sections.summary: The proposed method was validated on visual servoing of a 2-DOF gimbal driven by series elastic actuators (SEAs). Monte Carlo simulations verified the theoretical constraint violation rate (4.10%), achieved over 80% reduction in tracking error compared to a baseline, and clocked an average computation time of 2.0 ms.
sections.details:
For evaluation, the authors chose a highly nonlinear 2-DOF flexible gimbal involving Coriolis forces, centrifugal forces, gravity imbalance, and joint elastic vibrations. The task was to track a cloverleaf reference trajectory on the image plane (Figure F2) under camera FOV limits (pan $\pm 38^\circ$, tilt $\pm 30^\circ$) and actuator torque limits ($\pm 3.0\text{ Nm}$). Dropout transition probabilities were set to severe levels: $p_{01}=0.15$ and $p_{11}=0.8$ (an 80% chance of an outage continuing once started).

### Statistical Validation (Monte Carlo Simulations)
For a confidence level of $p=0.95$, the theoretical safety radius was $R_{prob} = 10.33^\circ$. Across 300 independent trials, the empirical 95th-percentile tracking error was $9.63^\circ$, falling safely within the theoretical bound. Furthermore, the constraint violation rate across all simulation steps was $4.10\%$, comfortably satisfying the design risk tolerance (below $5\%$).

### Tracking Performance and Comparative Evaluation
The proposed method achieved a root-mean-square error (RMSE) of $1.5^\circ$ on the pan axis and $1.8^\circ$ on the tilt axis. Thanks to open-loop predictions from the nominal linear model during measurement gaps, the mean absolute error (MAE) remained steady at $1.2^\circ$ and $1.6^\circ$.
As a baseline, they tested a switched PD controller that applies a zero-order hold (ZOH) on the previous control input during dropouts. With this baseline, MAE during dropouts surged to $6.9^\circ$ and $5.1^\circ$. The proposed method slashed dropout errors by $82.6\%$ on pan and $68.6\%$ on tilt compared to the baseline, achieving up to an $82.1\%$ improvement in overall RMSE.

Computation speed was equally remarkable. Because the problem is formulated as a convex quadratic program (QP), the solver's median computation time per step was only $2.0\text{ ms}$. This easily fits within the system's $50\text{ Hz}$ ($20\text{ ms}$) control cycle, proving the framework is fast enough for practical deployment on edge microcontrollers.

captions.F3: Figure F3 illustrates the maximum prediction error (vertical axis) alongside the step-wise constraint violation rate (color map) across 300 Monte Carlo runs. The vast majority of runs keep constraint violations down to a few percent, visually confirming that the overall average violation rate of 4.10% meets the design target (below 5%).

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps
sections.summary: For nonlinear systems subject to sensor dropouts, this work established an MPC framework integrating deep Koopman linearization, Markov jump boundedness proofs, and probabilistically truncated soft constraints for recursive feasibility. Fast convex optimization paves the way for real-time control on edge devices.
sections.details: This study presented an MPC strategy that simultaneously guarantees stability and recursive feasibility for constrained nonlinear systems exposed to stochastic measurement outages. By eliminating nonconvex optimization through a Lipschitz-constrained deep Koopman model and capturing measurement intermittency as a Markov jump system, the authors derived probabilistic safety radii and exact-penalty soft constraints. Numerical experiments demonstrated that excellent nonlinear tracking performance can be achieved alongside high execution speeds of 2 ms.

takeaways: Combining a deep Koopman operator with spectral normalization safely lifts nonlinear systems into latent linear models while preserving Lipschitz continuity, creating a highly practical setup for fast QP solving.

Formulating dropouts (open-loop expansion) and recoveries (state resets) as a Markov jump system allows prediction error mean-square ultimate boundedness (MSUB) to be elegantly proved via Lyapunov analysis.

Truncating tube tightening with a probabilistic bound and absorbing state jumps through exact-penalty soft constraints provides a powerful design pattern to prevent MPC infeasibility under intermittent feedback.
limitations: Under extreme outage conditions where the probability of dropouts persisting ($p_{11}$) approaches 1, the feasible region meeting safety constraints will vanish, reaching a theoretical limit (the paper also notes restrictions tied to maximum open-loop duration $l_{max}$).

Because the probabilistic safety boundary is derived using Markov's inequality, it offers distribution-free generality but yields a somewhat conservative radius ($10.33^\circ$ versus the empirical 95th percentile of $9.63^\circ$).

The approach has only been validated in simulation; evaluating its behavior when camera and motor disturbances, time delays, and identification errors interact on physical hardware remains future work.
